name: Vantablack Media Distributed Echo Mesh Kit
product_name: Vantablack Media Distributed Echo Mesh Kit
description:
The Distributed Echo Mesh Kit is a field-deployable mesh networking system packaged as a set of twelve adhesive node discs, each approximately the diameter of a coin and 4mm thick. When placed on surfaces throughout a building, tunnel system, or urban block, the nodes self-organize into a low-power mesh network within ninety seconds, creating a private encrypted communications backbone entirely independent of any existing infrastructure. The mesh operates on frequency-hopping spread spectrum in the sub-GHz band, prioritizing wall penetration and range over bandwidth. The resulting network supports voice, text, and low-resolution positional data for up to eight simultaneous users.

Vantablack Media developed the Echo Mesh Kit ostensibly for their field journalism teams operating in communications-denied environments — protest zones, disaster areas, and regions where corporate or state actors have seized control of local networks. The kit's civilian packaging and media-company branding have allowed it to circulate with relatively light regulatory scrutiny despite capabilities that make it extremely useful for operations that have nothing to do with journalism. Each node is designed to be nearly invisible once placed, with a matte surface that accepts paint, dust, and grime naturally.

The mesh has no central node — if any individual disc is found and destroyed, the network reroutes automatically. Full network collapse requires removal of nine or more of the twelve nodes. The discs are designed to be left behind: they are cheap enough to be considered disposable, and they self-wipe after a factory-set duration between 24 hours and 30 days depending on the configuration selected before deployment.

specifications.range_per_node_hop: Up to 120m in open space; 40m through reinforced concrete
specifications.power_source: Integrated micro-battery per node; non-rechargeable, single-use

tactical_use: Teams deploy the Echo Mesh Kit before entering a target building or zone, scattering nodes as they move through the space. Once the mesh is live, the team operates on a private network that exists entirely within the physical bounds of the deployment — no signal leaves the mesh perimeter in any meaningful form, and no external network access is required. This makes it invaluable in environments where the local network infrastructure has been compromised or is actively monitored. Nodes are placed in inconspicuous locations: inside ventilation grilles, under furniture, on the backs of doors. A standard sweep by corporate security rarely finds more than two or three before the team has completed its objective.
cultural_context: The Echo Mesh Kit is ubiquitous enough to have become mundane in certain circles — protest organizers, squatter communities, and underground venue operators all use it to maintain communications during events they expect authorities to disrupt. Vantablack's branding has given the kit a kind of countercultural legitimacy; owning one signals that you operate in spaces where the official network cannot be trusted. More sophisticated users treat the disposable nodes as a philosophy as much as a tool: build what you need, use it, leave it behind. Nothing you create has to be permanent.
known_users: Infiltration teams and corporate espionage operatives
story_hooks: A mesh network left behind after a job is still active weeks later — someone is using the nodes the team left behind, and they are transmitting something the team was never supposed to see.
A pattern emerges: every major incident in the Undercroft district over the past year has been preceded by an Echo Mesh deployment in the same three-block radius.
A character finds a single Echo Mesh node in their apartment that they did not place — the self-wipe timer has been disabled, and it has been active for six months.
Vantablack Media issues a firmware update that reduces the self-wipe window to a maximum of 48 hours, citing 'environmental responsibility.' The real reason is considerably more sinister.

A derelict building slated for demolition turns out to be the center of an ancient Echo Mesh network still running on the last of its battery reserves — the transmissions contain records of something that was never meant to be found.

physical_description.visual_profile: A sleek deployable mesh networking system consisting of twelve identical adhesive disc nodes. Each disc is a minimalist engineering statement—a flat, featureless black circle with a barely-perceptible metallic sheen that catches light only at extreme angles. The discs appear almost anti-design in their simplicity, intentionally forgettable.
physical_description.dimensions: Individual nodes: 28mm diameter (roughly the size of a UK pound coin or US quarter), 4mm thick. Complete kit in carrying case: approximately 120mm × 80mm × 30mm (slightly larger than a hardcover book).
physical_description.weight_description: Extremely lightweight and pocketable. Individual nodes: 4g each. Complete kit with carry case: under 150g. Can be carried in a jacket pocket or messenger bag without notice.
physical_description.primary_material: Housing: aerospace-grade polymer composite. Adhesive backing: pressure-sensitive acrylic gel (designed to bond without leaving residue). Antenna array: etched into interior circuit board.
physical_description.finish: Matte Vantablack-derived coating with near-zero reflectivity. Surface is designed to accept environmental contamination—dust, grime, paint, and weathering make nodes blend seamlessly with surroundings. Minimal logo marking on one face.
physical_description.color_scheme: Primary: deep charcoal black with near-imperceptible gradient. Accent: barely-visible Subliminal Overlay Division logo in dark gray on one side. No LED indicators or status lights—visual silence by design.
physical_description.interface_elements: Minimal. No buttons, screens, or ports on individual nodes. Configuration is handled through a paired handheld interface device (not shown) via NFC tap-pairing before deployment. Pre-deployment setup includes: deployment duration timer (mechanical dial, 1-3cm diameter) on the carry case, encrypted key storage, and a small handheld OLED status unit (approximately 8cm × 6cm) for network verification.
distinctive_features: Pressure-sensitive adhesive backing allows placement on any clean surface—walls, ceilings, conduits, under furniture
Flat disc form factor designed to disappear visually; can be covered by paint or stickers
Absence of any LEDs or status indicators—network operation is entirely invisible
Carrier case features minimalist industrial design: matte black anodized aluminum or polymer with discreet Vantablack Media branding
Self-wipe mechanism—no physical trigger or indicator; nodes simply stop transmitting after configured timer expires
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Subliminal Overlay Division (parent company: Vantablack Media) — small embossed logo on one face of each node. Serial batch codes on carry case. Regulatory compliance markings present but minimal and non-conspicuous.
physical_description.condition_typical: Fresh from the case: pristine matte black finish, adhesive backing protected by thin release liner. In-field: nodes rapidly accumulate dust, fingerprints, paint overspray, and environmental grime, rendering them nearly invisible. Deployed nodes show no signs of active operation—no heat signature, no electromagnetic emissions detectable at operating distance, no acoustic signature.
